info.title: Chronologity API
info.description:
Chronologity preserves and navigates personal and shared history as chronological Moments.

Two things shape almost every endpoint here, and a client that does not know them will be wrong:

**A 404 is not proof of absence.** Something you may not see and something that does not exist answer identically, deliberately. The same is true of authentication: no endpoint discloses whether an address, handle, or number belongs to an account.

**Chronology comes from when something happened, never from when it was recorded.** A Moment entered today for 2014 belongs in 2014, and occurrence is an interval at the precision it is actually known at rather than a fabricated instant.

bearerAuth.description:
The access token returned by any of the three sign-in routes.

Sent as `Authorization: Bearer <token>`. A token that verifies is not sufficient on its own: the Session it names must still be open, so signing out takes effect immediately rather than when the token expires.

get.description: Answers only whether this process is alive. It says nothing about whether the instance can serve traffic — a database outage must not cause an orchestrator to kill a healthy process.
Reports each dependency this instance needs. `degraded` with a 503 means traffic should go elsewhere; the process is still healthy and should not be restarted.

post.description: Answers identically whether or not an account exists. No authentication surface here discloses membership, because knowing that an address, handle, or number has an account is itself a fact about a person.
Sends a code to prove the number is yours. Claiming replaces whatever number the account held before, and the replacement starts unverified.

get.summary: Read the number on your account
get.description: `dormant` says the number has gone unused long enough to stop working for sign-in until confirmed again. You are told because you are the only person who can act on it.

delete.description: Removing one you do not have is the state you asked for, not an error.

post.description: A wrong code, an expired one, one already used, and one guessed at too often are all the same refusal. Enough wrong guesses spend the code, whether or not the right one arrives afterwards.

post.summary: Send a sign-in code by text
post.description: Answers identically whether or not an account exists. No authentication surface here discloses membership, because knowing that an address, handle, or number has an account is itself a fact about a person. A number that has gone unused for a long period receives no code at all; the account's email address is told instead, because a number left unused is the one a carrier may have given to somebody else.

post.summary: Sign in with a number and code
post.description: Succeeding emails the account, so its holder learns of it even if the number was taken from them.

An expired link, an already-used one, one issued for another purpose, and one that never existed are all the same refusal. Redeeming proves control of the address, so a first-time address arrives already verified.

get.description: The session making the request is marked as such.

delete.description: Including the one making the request.

post.description: Refresh tokens rotate: the one sent is spent, and a new one comes back. Reusing a spent token ends the session, because reuse means it was copied.

delete.description: Takes effect on that session's next request rather than at its next expiry.

post.description: Answers identically whether or not an account exists. Registering does not prove the address — redeeming the link sent to it does — and password sign-in is refused until it is proven.
Proving an address grants no session. Proof of who somebody is and being signed in are deliberately separate.

Answers identically whether or not an account exists. No such account, a wrong password, and an unproven address are one refusal — and the work is done either way, so the time taken says nothing either.
Answers identically whether or not an account exists.

post.summary: Set a new password with a reset link
post.description: Every other session ends, because a reset usually means the old password was known to somebody else.

put.description: Requires the current one. Every other session ends; the one making the change continues.

post.description: Authenticating proves who somebody is; it does not give them an account. Until this succeeds a caller holds an Identity, and every route needing a User answers 403 with `ONBOARDING_REQUIRED`.

patch.summary: Change your display name or biography

put.description: Handles are unique on their normalised form, so two people claiming one name at the same moment cannot both succeed. A released handle is reserved for a cooldown and may be reclaimed by its previous holder within it.

post.description: Ends every session and hides the account. Reversible by signing in again and reactivating; this is not deletion, and nothing recorded is removed.

Sends a confirmation link to your verified email address. Nothing is deleted until you use it.

**Deletion cannot be undone.** Your Moments, their photographs and videos, your comments, and your reactions are all removed. If you only want to step away for a while, deactivate instead.

The link exists because a signed-in session proves somebody signed in once, which an unattended laptop also proves. Using it proves you can read the mailbox now. The mail arriving is itself the protection: somebody who has taken your account over cannot delete it without this reaching you.

Asking twice sends a second link and cancels neither — otherwise anybody who could reach this could stop your deletion by asking again.

post.summary: Confirm that you want your account deleted
post.description:
Takes the token from the confirmation link. Your account stops working immediately: every session ends, your addresses and password are removed, and your handle is released after a cooldown.

What you recorded is removed afterwards rather than instantly, because a history of ten thousand Moments takes real work to erase. It is removed whether or not you are watching.

A link issued for a different account, one already used, one that has expired, and one of another purpose all refuse identically.

post.summary: Ask for a copy of your history
post.description:
Sends a confirmation link to your verified email address. Nothing is prepared until you use it.

The link exists for the same reason deletion has one: an export is everything you have, and a signed-in session only shows that somebody signed in once. Using it shows you can read the mailbox now, and the mail arriving means a stranger holding your session cannot quietly take a copy of your history.

get.description:
Reports how far along your export is and, once it is ready, where to fetch it.

**Every link in the manifest is signed when you ask and lives for minutes.** A link signed when the export was built would still work days later, which is the same as having no expiry at all.

Your photographs and videos are not copied to prepare an export — the manifest points at the originals. Media for a Moment you have since deleted is absent, because the manifest is built from what you have now rather than from what you had then.

A prepared export is removed after a few days.

post.summary: Confirm that you want your history prepared
post.description: Takes the token from the confirmation link and starts the work. A large history takes a while; check back with the endpoint below. Confirming while one is already being prepared changes nothing.

get.description: The only route here needing no caller. It carries nothing a person has not chosen to present.
The caller's own capabilities, resolved from their roles. Useful for deciding what to show; never for deciding what to allow. Every permission is enforced again server-side on the operation itself.

put.description: Requires `admin:user-role-manage`. Nobody may grant a role to themselves, and every attempt is recorded whether it succeeded or not — a refused self-escalation is exactly what a later review wants to find.

post.summary: Register an upload and get somewhere to put it
post.description: Returns a short-lived URL to PUT the bytes to directly. Large media never travels through the API. Nothing is trusted from this request: the declared content type and size are checked against the file itself once it arrives.

get.description: Paged by cursor. The cursor is opaque: it encodes where the ordering continues from, and taking it apart will break when the ordering changes.

post.description: Verifies the object is really there, then queues it for checking. An upload reaches `ready` only after a decoder has opened it and found it to be what it claimed — until then it cannot represent a Moment.

delete.description: Removes the stored object as well as the record.

get.description: Read from the file each time and kept nowhere. The position itself is never returned — it is used to ask what is nearby, and the named places are what the owner chooses from. A photograph knowing where it was taken does not make that a fact about somebody's history.

Asks the map service for candidates. Nothing here exists in Chronologity yet — a suggestion becomes a Location only when somebody records one from it, and the name it is recorded with is kept forever rather than re-fetched later.

post.description: Recording the same map result twice reaches the same Location rather than creating a second one. A Location is shared reference data: recording it is provenance, not ownership, and anybody's Moment may point at it.

A shared occurrence a Moment may have been part of — a concert, a moon landing, a wedding. Identity never depends on the title alone, so duplicates are expected before anybody reconciles them and two Events with one name stay distinct.

Chronology comes from `occurrence`, never from when this was called: a Moment entered today for 2014 belongs in 2014. Occurrence is an interval at the precision it is actually known at, so a summer stays a summer rather than acquiring a fabricated day. Media is required and must already be `ready`.

get.description: Everything you recorded, at every visibility, newest occurrence first. Paged by cursor; the cursor is opaque and taking it apart will break when the ordering changes.

patch.description: Every change is kept, with what the thing was before.

get.description: `place` reflects what you in particular may be told about where this happened: below `exact` it carries no identifier and no coordinates, so what was withheld cannot be looked up.

put.description: Its own operation, separate from a caption: moving a Moment through chronology is a historical correction, and a caption is enrichment.
Presentation only. It never moves the Moment through chronology.

delete.description: Removing the last one is refused: media is required, so it would leave a Moment that could not have been created. Deleting the Moment is a different operation.

put.description: Replaces whatever was said before. One place per Moment: media pointing at several distinct places usually means several Moments.

delete.description: The Moment survives losing its place. Removing context is not removing history.

post.description: Several are permitted, unlike places: a photograph at a wedding that is also part of a family reunion is genuinely both.

put.summary: Set whether it may be recommended
put.description: Separate from who may see it. Unlisting leaves a Moment reachable by anybody you give the link to and takes it out of every recommendation surface — Chronologity will not put it in front of somebody who did not ask. Public Moments are discoverable unless you say otherwise.

Visibility and audience together, so a Moment is never restricted with a list left from an earlier decision. An audience is accepted only with `restricted`. Changing visibility never moves the Moment through chronology.

put.summary: Set how much of the place others are told
put.description: A different question from the Location's own `precision`, which says how well anybody knows where this happened. This says how much of that another Viewer receives. You always see the exact place yourself.

get.summary: Read who may see a restricted Moment
get.description: The author's own list. Being on it does not entitle somebody to read it.

post.summary: Claim a relationship to another Moment
post.description: A claim somebody made, never something derived from chronological order: that one Moment preceded another says nothing about why. One of the two Moments must be your own. A causal claim contradicting the known times is refused, though an order nobody can establish is allowed.

get.description: A relationship whose other end you may not see is absent entirely rather than returned with the identifier blanked, because the identifier is itself the disclosure.

delete.description: Only whoever made a claim may withdraw it: owning one end does not make somebody else's reading of history yours to retract. Both Moments are left exactly as they were.

put.description: Replaces whatever you left before; you hold at most one reaction per Moment, so the total counts you once. A Moment not accepting reactions and an author who has blocked you answer the same way, because naming a block would tell somebody they had been blocked.

delete.description: Permitted even where reacting is not, so somebody blocked afterwards — or reacting before the author turned reactions off — can still withdraw. Withdrawing one you never left is the state you asked for, not an error.

get.summary: How a Moment has been responded to
get.description: Counts by kind, the number of people, and your own. Never who else reacted. `enabled: false` means the author turned reactions off and the counts are withheld — which is a different fact from nobody having reacted, and worth rendering differently. Counts are derived and may lag; they are engagement, never historical importance.

put.description: Turning them off hides the existing counts as well as refusing new ones. Nothing is deleted: turning them back on brings the same counts back.

post.description: Conversation, not history: when this was written says nothing about when the Moment happened, and nothing here moves it. Supply `commentId` to make a retry safe — the same identifier twice yields one comment, while the same text twice without one yields two, because repeating yourself deliberately is allowed. Replying to a reply joins that reply's thread rather than nesting deeper.

get.description: Top-level comments, oldest first, and never ranked by engagement. `total` counts replies too. A deleted comment with replies appears as a tombstone carrying neither body nor author, so the replies still have something to hang from; one without replies is simply gone.
Replies to a top-level comment, oldest first.

patch.description: Marks the comment edited and leaves its place in the conversation alone — editing must not become a way of moving up the discussion.

delete.description: Leaves the Moment untouched. If replies hang from it, a tombstone remains so the conversation still reads; if none do, it disappears.

put.summary: Set who may join the discussion
put.description: `anyone` who can see the Moment, `followers` of its author, or `disabled`. Closing a discussion refuses new comments and leaves what was already said readable — removing it would be a separate act. The author may always comment on their own Moment.

The same four kinds a Moment takes. A Moment's own reaction setting does not reach its discussion: silencing reactions to a photograph should not silence agreement between people talking underneath it.

delete.summary: Take a reaction to a comment back

put.summary: Say this Moment matters to you
put.description: Private, always — nobody sees anybody else's mark, and no response anywhere carries one. You may mark any Moment you can see, including one somebody else recorded: the last photograph of a loved one may have been taken by a sibling. Two people marking the same Moment is not a conflict; each mark belongs to its own history. Marking twice is the state already holding.

delete.description: Unmarking one you never marked is the state you asked for, not an error.

get.description: Your own mark and nothing else. Which Moments matter to somebody is closer to a diary than to a reaction, so there is no way to ask whether anybody else marked one.
Only the Moments you may see. Pages are full rather than thinned after the fact, so a short page means the end rather than that something was removed. Asking for your own returns everything.

post.summary: Say somebody was part of this Moment
post.description:
Proposes participation. Only the Moment's creator may propose, and only the person named may establish it — until they answer, this asserts nothing and is visible to the two of you alone.

**You may propose in a Moment they cannot read.** They are told who asked and when it happened, and nothing else: not the caption, not the media, not the place, not who else was there. Requiring you to admit somebody before asking them would make over-sharing the price of consent.

A Moment names at most 100 people, counting unanswered proposals — a proposal holds its place.

**A refusal is silent.** Somebody who has blocked you, or who has refused proposals from you, answers exactly as an account that does not exist. Refusing exists so a person can stop being asked, and telling the asker they were refused hands them what they need to ask another way.

get.summary: Who this Moment records as having been there
get.description:
People who confirmed they were part of it. Unanswered proposals are never listed here, whoever is asking: a proposal is a question between two people, and reaching it through the Moment would answer it for everybody else.

Readable by anybody who may read the Moment, and by nobody who may not.

post.description:
Establishes the participation. Only the person named may do this.

**Accepting grants you nothing.** If you could not read the Moment before, you still cannot. If you want to see it, ask its author — that decision is theirs and stays theirs.

post.summary: Say you were not part of this
post.description:
Refuses the proposal, and refuses it permanently: the creator may never propose you for that Moment again.

A refusal that can be repeated is not a refusal, it is a delay. Somebody asked again each week has no control, only a recurring task.

The creator is told you refused, rather than left to wonder — somebody who cannot tell refusal from silence will ask again outside the product.

delete.summary: Withdraw from a Moment, or take back a proposal
delete.description:
Two acts with the same verb, told apart by who is asking and what state the participation is in.

**A participant withdraws** something they accepted, and that is permanent — the creator may never propose them for that Moment again, exactly as a refusal.

**A creator takes back** a proposal nobody has answered. That is not a refusal, so it leaves nothing behind and they may ask again. A creator cannot remove a participation somebody accepted: that record belongs to the person who confirmed it, and the recourse is to delete the Moment.

get.description:
`to-me` lists what other people have said about you, which you may answer. `by-me` lists what you have said about others, which you may take back while it is unanswered.

Two directions rather than one list, because they are different screens with different actions.
Only your own, and only the direction you can act on. Who has refused **you** is not something this product will tell you, for the same reason a Block is never announced.

post.description:
Stops this person asking you to confirm you were anywhere. Weaker than a Block, which severs everything in both directions; this covers the ordinary case, where somebody is not blocked but is not welcome to keep asking.

Participations you already accepted are untouched. A refusal governs what may be asked from here, not what you already agreed to.

delete.description: Lets them ask again from here. Restores nothing: proposals settled while the refusal stood stay settled, as a Block's severing does.

post.summary: Keep the view you are looking at
post.description:
Stores what you are looking at — the context, the lens, the stretch of time, where you had got to — under a name you choose.

**What is kept is the view, not the Moments.** Reopening it next year derives history as it stands then, so a view of a place shows what has been added to it since, and a view of "this year" means whichever year you open it in.

Keeping a view grants you nothing. It is authorised afresh each time it is opened, so a Moment that is public today and private tomorrow simply stops appearing.

get.description: Newest first. Each carries its specification, so a client can show what a view is about — a place, a decade, a lens — without deriving it.
The view and what it is about. Somebody else's reads as absent rather than refused, so identifiers cannot be probed.

patch.description:
Changes what it is called and nothing else.

**What it points at cannot be edited.** A view that pointed somewhere new would be a different view wearing an old name, and anybody holding a link to it would be given something they were never shown. Save another one instead.

delete.description: Removes it, and every link you made to it. A link to a view that no longer exists stops opening.

put.description:
Asks to be told when Moments matching this view are added — including old ones, since somebody scanning a shoebox of 1994 negatives is exactly the addition worth hearing about.

**Following is a second act, not a consequence of saving.** Saving keeps a perspective to come back to; this asks to be told without looking.

You are told once per view until you open it, however much arrives. What you are told is that there is more to see — never what, because a sentence naming it would be composed now and read later by somebody whose access may have narrowed since.

delete.description: The view is kept and stops telling you about itself. Anything already sent stays where it is.

post.summary: Say you have looked at a view
post.description:
Records that you opened this view and explored it, which is what the count of new Moments is measured from. Everything recorded after this point is what you have not seen.

**Call it when somebody actually looks, not when you list.** Listing views is not looking at one, and clearing the count because a list was prefetched would lose somebody the only signal they had that their history had grown.

post.summary: Make a link to a saved view
post.description:
Creates a link somebody else can open. They see the view — the place, the range, the lens — derived **for them**.

**Sharing confers no access.** Two people opening one link see different Moments, each seeing only what they were already entitled to, and neither learns what the other saw. A view full of your private history shows a stranger nothing at all.

**You choose what the link says about you.** By default it names neither the title nor you: a title is your words about your own history, and a link outlives the conversation you sent it in. One view can be shared twice on different terms.

The token is returned once here and readable afterwards from your own list of shares.

get.summary: Links you have made to a saved view
get.description: Including ones you have withdrawn, so you can see what you gave out and what you took back.

delete.description: The link stops opening. Anybody still holding it is told there is no such shared view, which is what a token that never existed is told — a withdrawn link should not confirm to a guesser that it once worked.

get.summary: Open a link somebody sent you
get.description:
Returns the view: a context, a stretch of time, a lens. Not any history — you then read it through the Timeline as yourself, which is what stops a shared link ever showing you a Moment you could not otherwise open.

Whether it names the view or the person who saved it is their choice, and by default it names neither.

post.description: The answer says which happened, so nothing has to expose in advance whether an account requires approval. Following somebody you already follow succeeds: you asked for a state that already holds. An account that has blocked you answers as though it does not exist.

delete.description: Unfollowing somebody you never followed is not an error.
The same relationship as unfollowing, ended from the other side. Kept separate because they are different acts: one is losing interest, the other is withdrawing an audience.

post.description: One act: the block is recorded, any follow in either direction is removed, and any pending request between you is cancelled. Nothing tells the other person. Blocking somebody already blocked is the state already holding.

delete.description: Restores nothing. What the block severed stays severed, and either of you may follow again from scratch.

get.description: Only the direction you can act on. There is no way to learn who has blocked you, because the product must not tell anybody that.

post.description: No approval: an Event is shared history, so there is nobody to ask. Following grants no access to anything — it says what you want to hear about, never what you may see.
No approval: a Location is shared reference data. An interface may present this as following a timeline.

get.description: Paged by cursor. The cursor is opaque: it encodes where the ordering continues from, and taking it apart will break when the ordering changes.

post.description: Creates the follow and settles the request together.
Kept rather than deleted, so what was asked and refused survives.

Available to anybody signed in. A report changes nothing by itself: report volume may affect how soon a moderator looks, and never establishes that anything broke a rule. The person reported is never told who reported them. Reporting the same thing twice returns the report already filed rather than failing.

get.description: Your own reports and where each has got to. Carries no reviewer identity, no internal detail, and nothing about the person reported.
Status only. A report somebody else filed is reported as absent rather than forbidden: that a report exists about a given subject is itself something you are not entitled to learn.

post.description: A separate path from safety reporting, and a separate queue. Saying a Moment happened in 2004 rather than 2005 is a correction; saying it threatens you is not. Nothing filed here can reach a moderation state.

get.description: Your own historical-accuracy reports and where each has got to.

get.summary: What was done to your content
get.description: Every moderation decision taken against your own content, with the reason and whether you have appealed it. This is what makes an appeal possible: nobody can contest a decision they were never told about. Attempts that were refused are not listed — those are evidence for a security review rather than something that happened to you.

post.description: Appeal a moderation decision taken against you. Available while suspended, since an enforcement system somebody cannot answer is not one. A decision already under appeal is refused rather than silently ignored, because an appeal carries a statement you wrote.

get.description: Outcome included once there is one. Somebody else's appeal reads as absent.

Requires `moderation:report-review`. Oldest first, so nothing waits indefinitely behind newer arrivals. Each report carries how many separate people reported the subject and whether they arrived together — both to inform a reviewer, neither to decide anything.
Requires `moderation:report-review`. Carries the reporter, which the subject never receives.

put.summary: Move a report through its status
put.description: Requires `moderation:report-review`. Deciding a report and moderating its subject are separate acts: a report can be closed with nothing done, because no violation is a real outcome. Resolved and closed are terminal.

get.description: Requires `moderation:report-review`. Holds no safety reports: they live in a different table, so the separation is structural rather than a filter somebody could forget.

put.description: Requires `moderation:report-review`. Reaches no moderation state: a wrong date is something to fix, not something to enforce against, and the correction itself belongs to the Moment's author.

Requires `moderation:content-moderate`. Decides what Chronologity distributes, never what happened: occurrence, authorship, and position in chronology are untouched, the author keeps reading their own, and nothing is deleted. Setting `allowed` clears the state. Moderating a Moment's last remaining medium makes the Moment itself unavailable, because a Moment without media could not have been created. An attempt by somebody without the permission is recorded before it is refused.

Requires `moderation:account-suspend`. Hides what the account contributed and deletes none of it: follows, blocks, relationships, Moments, and comments all survive, because the account may come back. The suspended person keeps reading their own history and may appeal. An attempt by somebody without the permission is recorded before it is refused.

get.description: Requires `moderation:appeal-review`. Oldest first.

put.description: Requires `moderation:appeal-review`. Reversing restores what the action restricted — which is possible only because moderation hid things rather than destroying them.

get.description:
Searches Moments, accounts, real-world Events, and Locations at once; `type` narrows it to one. Every result carries what it is.

**A result is a pointer, not a permission.** Opening one reauthorizes against current state — a result you saw a minute ago may refuse to open, and that is the system working rather than failing.

**Nothing is ranked by popularity.** Reactions and comments are not signals here. Historical significance breaks ties between comparably good matches and never promotes a weak one, and no score is returned: a number beside a result reads as a judgement about the past.

**Occurrence precision is preserved.** A Moment known only as 'summer 1998' is found by a search for 1998 and does not acquire an invented date to make the comparison easier. Temporal filters overlap rather than contain.

**Proximity is answered at the granularity the author allowed.** `geoPrecision` in the response says which — a 200 metre radius cannot be honoured for a Moment whose author shared only the city, and rather than rounding that away silently, the response says what it could actually do. A Moment with its place hidden is never a proximity match.

**A cursor belongs to one search.** Sending one from a different query, or from before a ranking change, is refused rather than silently restarted or re-ordered mid-page.

Zero results means zero results. Nothing loosely related is substituted to avoid an empty answer.

Suggests accounts, real-world Events, and Locations for a prefix — the things you navigate to. **Moments are never suggested.** A caption is the most sensitive text Chronologity holds, and a surface that answers every keystroke is the worst place to put it; finding a Moment is what `/search` is for.

**Suggestions obey exactly the same eligibility rule as results, not a looser one.** A private entity's name must not surface because somebody typed three letters that happen to match it. The same predicate decides both, so the two cannot drift apart.

A suggestion carries a name and an identifier and nothing else — no snippet, no caption, no occurrence. Where an alias matched, the response says so and gives the name the thing normally goes by, since 'The Great War' on its own looks like a different Event.

Fewer than two characters returns an empty list rather than an error: a box somebody is still typing into has not done anything wrong, and answering one letter would turn this into a listing of everything they may see. Rate limited more tightly than search, because walking the alphabet through it is a way of asking what exists.

Public history, offered to anybody. Not personalised and not assembled from anything you have looked at — which is also why a new account sees the same page as an old one.

**Being able to see something is not permission to be shown it.** Everything here passes the access rule Search uses and is then narrowed further: it must be public, its author must have left it discoverable, moderation must permit amplification, and its author must be an adult. A restricted Moment is never recommended — not even to somebody on its list — and a private one is never recommended, including to its own author.

**Nothing is ranked by popularity.** Reactions, comments, and views are not signals, and the ranking code cannot reach them. Explore orders by derived historical significance, used as context rather than as a universal score, and no score is returned.

**No one voice fills a page.** How much any single author, place, or Event may occupy is capped, so a page may come back shorter than asked for. That is the cap working rather than a shortage.

**Every result says why it was offered.** Each reason describes the recommendation itself, so an explanation can never disclose more than the recommendation already does.

What people recorded of a real-world Event. An Event with no history you may be offered returns an empty page rather than a refusal: that the Event exists is not a secret, and how much of its history reaches you is.

**Being able to see something is not permission to be shown it.** Everything here passes the access rule Search uses and is then narrowed further: it must be public, its author must have left it discoverable, moderation must permit amplification, and its author must be an adult. A restricted Moment is never recommended — not even to somebody on its list — and a private one is never recommended, including to its own author.

**Nothing is ranked by popularity.** Reactions, comments, and views are not signals, and the ranking code cannot reach them. Explore orders by derived historical significance, used as context rather than as a universal score, and no score is returned.

**No one voice fills a page.** How much any single author, place, or Event may occupy is capped, so a page may come back shorter than asked for. That is the cap working rather than a shortage.

**Every result says why it was offered.** Each reason describes the recommendation itself, so an explanation can never disclose more than the recommendation already does.

What happened somewhere. Answered at the granularity each Moment's author disclosed, so a place somebody shared only at city level is reachable by a city-sized view and not a street-sized one.

**Being able to see something is not permission to be shown it.** Everything here passes the access rule Search uses and is then narrowed further: it must be public, its author must have left it discoverable, moderation must permit amplification, and its author must be an adult. A restricted Moment is never recommended — not even to somebody on its list — and a private one is never recommended, including to its own author.

**Nothing is ranked by popularity.** Reactions, comments, and views are not signals, and the ranking code cannot reach them. Explore orders by derived historical significance, used as context rather than as a universal score, and no score is returned.

**No one voice fills a page.** How much any single author, place, or Event may occupy is capped, so a page may come back shorter than asked for. That is the cap working rather than a shortage.

**Every result says why it was offered.** Each reason describes the recommendation itself, so an explanation can never disclose more than the recommendation already does.

History around a point. **Your position is query input and nothing else** — it is never stored as history, never becomes visible presence, and using this does not turn on location sharing of any kind.

As with Search, a radius is answered at the granularity the disclosures allow rather than being honoured exactly.

**Being able to see something is not permission to be shown it.** Everything here passes the access rule Search uses and is then narrowed further: it must be public, its author must have left it discoverable, moderation must permit amplification, and its author must be an adult. A restricted Moment is never recommended — not even to somebody on its list — and a private one is never recommended, including to its own author.

**Nothing is ranked by popularity.** Reactions, comments, and views are not signals, and the ranking code cannot reach them. Explore orders by derived historical significance, used as context rather than as a universal score, and no score is returned.

**No one voice fills a page.** How much any single author, place, or Event may occupy is capped, so a page may come back shorter than asked for. That is the cap working rather than a shortage.

**Every result says why it was offered.** Each reason describes the recommendation itself, so an explanation can never disclose more than the recommendation already does.

Other history connected to a Moment: relationships somebody asserted, the same real-world Event, or the same place.

**Nothing here is inferred.** Every connection was claimed by a person, and no similarity a model noticed is presented as though it were an established relationship.

**Being able to see something is not permission to be shown it.** Everything here passes the access rule Search uses and is then narrowed further: it must be public, its author must have left it discoverable, moderation must permit amplification, and its author must be an adult. A restricted Moment is never recommended — not even to somebody on its list — and a private one is never recommended, including to its own author.

**Nothing is ranked by popularity.** Reactions, comments, and views are not signals, and the ranking code cannot reach them. Explore orders by derived historical significance, used as context rather than as a universal score, and no score is returned.

**No one voice fills a page.** How much any single author, place, or Event may occupy is capped, so a page may come back shorter than asked for. That is the cap working rather than a shortage.

**Every result says why it was offered.** Each reason describes the recommendation itself, so an explanation can never disclose more than the recommendation already does.

Your notifications, newest first.

**Each is composed when you read it, from what you may see now.** Nothing is stored but identifiers, so a notification about something you can no longer see is simply absent rather than blanked — and a privacy change needs no propagation to reach it.

**Activity of one kind on one thing collapses while unread.** Three people reacting to a Moment is one entry, not three. Reading it starts a fresh one.

People are named only where you may know who they are; anybody else is counted instead. An aggregated notification is never a way to learn who somebody is.

A page may come back shorter than asked for, because entries you can no longer see were dropped. That is honest rather than a shortage.

Counted over what you can currently see, not over what exists. A count that outran the list would tell you something existed that the list had already decided not to show you. Bounded: past a hundred it reports a hundred.

**A notification is a pointer, never a permission.** Opening one resolves access again, so a notification about something since made private refuses to open rather than opening it. Somebody else's notification reads as absent rather than forbidden — that one exists is itself a disclosure about activity you are not party to.

put.description: Marking something already read succeeds: the state you asked for is the state that holds. Reading an aggregated entry also closes it, so later activity on the same thing opens a new one rather than growing this.
Dismissing marks it read as well. Somebody who has put something away has finished with it, and leaving it counted would be a badge nobody can clear.

get.description:
Every category on every channel.

`required` names the categories delivered whatever you choose — moderation, because being told what was done to your content is what makes appealing it possible, and security, because a preference that could silence "your password was changed" would be the first thing somebody taking over your account turned off.

**Switching a category off in-app silences its email and push too.** The in-app entry is the notification; the other channels carry it, and there is nothing to carry once it does not exist. The reverse does not hold: switching off email or push leaves the in-app entry standing.

put.description: A change to a required category is remembered and has no effect, rather than being refused — so an interface need not know which categories are fixed before sending, and the preference is honoured if the category ever stops being required. **A preference can never cause a notification you were not entitled to receive**: eligibility is decided before preferences are consulted.

post.description:
Registers this installation so push can reach it.

**The token is a credential, not an identifier.** Anybody holding it can send to the device, so it goes in and never comes back out: no response here or anywhere else carries it, and it is never written to a log.

Safe to call on every launch — the same token refreshes the existing registration rather than opening a second one. Registering a token another account currently holds moves it, and that account stops receiving: a phone can be handed on, and two people's private notifications must not arrive on one lock screen.

delete.description: What signing out on a device should do. Notification history stays in the account and nothing further arrives on that device. Somebody else's device reads as absent rather than forbidden — that one exists is a fact about an account you are not party to.

get.description: Separate from preferences, which say whether you hear about something at all. **These can only ever delay, never suppress**: a notification you cannot switch off still arrives when your quiet hours end rather than never. Hours are local to the time zone on your account.

put.description:
Per channel, because push and email want opposite answers: one is for what is worth interrupting you, the other for a summary.

A quiet window may run past midnight — `22` to `7` is quiet from 22:00 until 06:59. The opening hour is quiet and the closing hour is not, and the two ends must differ.

Account security ignores quiet hours entirely. By morning a stolen account may be gone, so that is the one thing worth waking you for; a moderation decision waits, because appealing it is no more possible at three than at eight.

tags.name: Authentication
tags.description: Proving who somebody is. Three methods reach one Identity: a link sent to an address, a password, and a code sent to a phone number.

tags.name: Users
tags.description: The account somebody chooses to present: handle, display name, preferences.

tags.name: Authorization
tags.description: Platform roles and what they permit. Roles never live in tokens.

tags.name: Uploads
tags.description: Media, uploaded straight to storage rather than through the API. What a file is comes from reading it, never from what the uploader said.

tags.name: Locations
tags.description: Places, as shared reference data. A place keeps the name it had when a Moment was recorded.

tags.name: Real-world Events
tags.description: Shared occurrences a Moment may have been part of.

tags.name: Moments
tags.description: Something that happened, at a time, recorded by one person. Media is evidence of the experience; the Moment is the experience.

tags.name: Social
tags.description: Following, requests, and blocking. Following says what somebody wants to hear about, never what they may see.
